---
title: "Mathematical detail"
---

Formulas used by `LongRunRisksModel`. Notation follows Kiku (2006)
unless noted. Collapsed callouts hold derivations.

## Euler equation

For any claim $i$ with gross return $R_{i,t+1}$,

$$
E_t\!\left[M_{t+1}\, R_{i,t+1}\right] = 1 .
$$ {#eq-euler}

$M_{t+1}$ is the pricing kernel. Once payoffs are weighted by the
state-by-state exchange rate, every asset earns its price. The same
condition prices a stock, a bill, and a private dividend stream.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Derivation"}
The investor maximizes $E_t \sum_j \delta^j u(C_{t+j})$. Reduce
consumption at $t$ by $\xi$, buy $\xi/P_t$ units of an asset with
payoff $X_{t+1}$, and consume the proceeds. At an optimum,
$u'(C_t)\,P_t = E_t[\delta\, u'(C_{t+1})\, X_{t+1}]$. Divide by
$u'(C_t)$ and by $P_t$, and set
$M_{t+1} = \delta\, u'(C_{t+1})/u'(C_t)$,
$R_{i,t+1} = X_{t+1}/P_t$.
:::

Power utility, $u(C) = C^{1-\gamma}/(1-\gamma)$, makes $M$ a function
of current consumption growth only. That kernel fails the equity
premium, the risk-free rate, and the value premium at once (Hansen and
Jagannathan 1991; Mehra and Prescott 1985). The failures are why the
family changes both preferences and the endowment.

## Epstein–Zin preferences

Lifetime utility is recursive (Epstein and Zin 1989):

$$
V_t = \left[(1-\delta)\, C_t^{\frac{1-\gamma}{\theta}}
      + \delta \left(E_t\!\left[V_{t+1}^{\,1-\gamma}\right]\right)^{\frac{1}{\theta}}
      \right]^{\frac{\theta}{1-\gamma}},
\qquad
\theta = \frac{1-\gamma}{1-\tfrac{1}{\psi}} .
$$ {#eq-ez}

Risk aversion $\gamma$ sits inside the certainty equivalent. The
elasticity of intertemporal substitution $\psi$ sits in the outer
aggregator. When $\gamma = 1/\psi$, $\theta = 1$ and the recursion is
power utility. Any other configuration is something power utility
cannot represent.

The log kernel (Kiku, eq. 5) is

$$
m_{t+1} = \theta \log \delta
          - \frac{\theta}{\psi}\, \Delta c_{t+1}
          + (\theta - 1)\, r_{c,t+1},
$$ {#eq-kernel}

where $r_{c,t+1}$ is the log return on the consumption claim. Marginal
utility depends on news about lifetime consumption, not only on this
month's $\Delta c$.

Table II sets $\delta = 0.999$, $\gamma = 10$, $\psi = 1.5$, so
$\theta = -9$. The household prefers early resolution of uncertainty.

## Endowment

$$
\Delta c_{t+1} = \mu_c + x_t + \sigma_t\, \eta_{t+1}
$$ {#eq-cons}

$$
x_{t+1} = \rho\, x_t + \varphi_x\, \sigma_t\, \epsilon_{t+1}
$$ {#eq-x}

$$
\sigma_{t+1}^2 = \bar\sigma^2 (1-\nu) + \nu\, \sigma_t^2 + \sigma_w\, w_{t+1}
$$ {#eq-vol}

$$
\Delta d_{i,t+1} = \mu_i + \phi_i\, x_t + \varphi_{\sigma,i}\, \sigma_t\, u_{i,t+1}
$$ {#eq-div}

with standard-normal shocks. $\phi_i$ is cash-flow leverage. Half-life
of a shock to $x_t$ is $\log(0.5)/\log(\rho)$, about 34 months at
$\rho = 0.98$.

## Log-linear solution

The log price-dividend ratio is taken to be affine in the state
(Campbell and Shiller 1988),

$$
z_t \equiv \log(P_t/D_t) = A_0 + A_1\, x_t + A_2\, \sigma_t^2 .
$$ {#eq-affine}

For a claim with leverage $\phi$ (Kiku, eq. 11),

$$
A_1 = \frac{\phi - \tfrac{1}{\psi}}{1 - \kappa_1 \rho},
$$ {#eq-a1}

where $\kappa_1 = e^{\bar z}/(1 + e^{\bar z})$ is a linearization
constant near one. Prices rise on good growth news when
$\phi > 1/\psi$. With $\psi = 1.5$ that threshold is $0.67$. The
denominator magnifies the numerator because $\rho$ is close to one.

`solve(method="analytical")` returns $A_1$, $A_2$, the long-run risk
premium, and the three shock prices. There is no return distribution
in this solution, so no volatilities and no betas.

## Quadrature solution

Tauchen and Hussey (1991) replace the continuous state with a Markov
chain on $(x_t, \sigma_t^2)$ and solve the Euler equation on the
chain. The paper uses 30 nodes for $x$ and 4 for $\sigma^2$.

The weighting density $\omega$ is scaled to the *unconditional*
distribution of $x$, so the nodes cover the states the process visits.
Scaling $\omega$ to the one-step conditional density at the mean
truncates the range and removes most of the value premium.

`solve()` (default `method="grid"`) is this solution. Population
moments are averages under the stationary distribution of the chain.
`simulate` is different: it is the cross-sample mean of statistics
computed on finite annual samples, which is Table VII.

The discretized economy is the economy you actually solve. Kiku's
printed Table VII return *levels* do not reproduce exactly from a
30-point grid; the gap is over-dispersion of $x$. Spreads and betas
are the objects the paper tests.

Source: Cochrane, *Asset Pricing*, ch. 1; Epstein and Zin (1989);
Bansal and Yaron (2004); Campbell and Shiller (1988); Tauchen and
Hussey (1991); Kiku (2006).
